skeptic.explanation: This is an impact crater rim and steep inner wall lit from the southwest/west. The dark narrow streaks on the bright wall are best read as slope streaks: dust avalanches that expose darker material beneath the bright dust mantle. They are common on dusty Arabia Terra slopes at this latitude. The fine, lighter radial lineations are mass-wasting textures on the wall.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The very high brightness of the inner wall compared with the outer plains is partly an effect of lighting geometry and contrast stretch. That makes it hard to tell albedo from slope. The thinness of some streaks could also be confused with small gullies at this resolution.
skeptic.would_refute: Repeat imaging showing the dark streaks unchanged in position, plus HiRISE showing incised channels with depositional aprons rather than surface tone changes with no relief, would point to gullies instead of slope streaks.

skeptic.explanation: This is a dust-mantled crater rim in the dusty Arabia Terra region. The dark tapering streak on the inner wall is a slope streak: a thin layer of bright dust slid down the steep wall and exposed darker material beneath. Its narrow downslope shape, sharp edges and point-like upslope origin, along with similar streaks elsewhere on the walls, fit this explanation. The floor texture is typical mid-latitude concentric crater fill. The smooth exterior is regional mantle draped over the rim and ejecta.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The exterior shows soft, blotchy tonal mottling that could be partly noise or contrast stretching, because the close view is noticeably grainy at this enlargement. It does not affect the main interpretation.
skeptic.would_refute: A later image of the same wall showing the dark streak unchanged in tone and exactly matched to bedrock outcrop or a topographic trough would argue against a slope streak. So would a streak that crosses the rim without following the downslope direction in an elevation model.

skeptic.landform_class: scarp / valley wall with slope streaks
skeptic.explanation: This is most likely the west-facing wall of a shallow valley or erosional scarp in dust-mantled Arabia Terra terrain, with the plain to the east standing higher. Illumination comes from the west: small craters show shadowed western inner walls and lit eastern inner walls. That lighting is consistent with the broad bright band being a sunlit slope descending westward from the crest. The thin dark, tapering streaks that start near the crest and run down this slope fit classic slope streaks, which form when dust avalanches on steep dusty slopes and are common in this region. The fainter bright streaks are likely older, faded slope streaks. The feature's curved, continuous form across both views argues against a camera artefact.
skeptic.does_not_fit: Without topography, it is uncertain whether this is a channel wall (fluvial valley) or a tectonic or erosional scarp. The small bench just east of the crest is not specifically explained. The brightness of the slope could partly reflect thicker dust rather than slope orientation alone.
skeptic.would_refute: An elevation model (CTX or HRSC DEM) showing the bright band is not a westward-descending slope, or that the eastern plain is not higher. Alternatively, an image under different sun azimuth in which the streaks do not follow the slope direction.

skeptic.explanation: This is a relatively young simple impact crater formed in a dust- or ice-rich mantled plain. Its circular plan, sharp rim and bowl profile, with a shadowed west wall and lit east wall under western illumination, are typical of a fresh simple crater. The concentric bands inside most likely come from layering in the target mantle exposed in the wall, or from slumping or modest infill. The NW–SE streaking around the crater fits wind sculpting of the surrounding fine-grained mantle. None of the patterns follow detector or mosaic geometry.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The concentric interior bands are ambiguous at this resolution. They could be exposed layers in the wall, slump terraces, or the start of concentric fill, and the image cannot separate these.
skeptic.would_refute: A CTX or HiRISE stereo elevation model showing the feature stands above the plain as a mound rather than sitting below it as a depression would refute the crater interpretation.

skeptic.explanation: The dark streaks are slope streaks: thin, dark, downslope-elongated markings formed when the bright dust mantle is disturbed and slides, exposing or creating darker surface. They are typical of steep, dust-covered slopes in low-thermal-inertia regions such as Arabia Terra. Their downslope orientation, tapering and branching shapes, and confinement to the dusty slope all fit. Differences between the CTX and HiRISE images, such as streaks that look fainter or are in other positions, are what you expect from slope streaks that fade over time and form anew.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The straight, vertical tonal boundaries in the HiRISE image (near x≈60 and x≈620 px) cut across the topography. They are best explained as CCD channel or stitch seams, an instrumental effect, not ground features.
skeptic.would_refute: Slope streaks should run strictly downslope. An elevation model showing the streaks running across contours or uphill would refute this, as would repeat imaging showing the streaks fixed and unchanging over decades with tonal relief that implies they are bedrock outcrops.

skeptic.explanation: This is the illuminated, sun-facing interior wall of an impact crater. The dark linear features are slope streaks: avalanche-like movements of bright dust that expose a darker substrate. Several features support this. The streaks are narrow, straight, and run directly downslope. They start near the rim crest and end above the floor, and they are confined to the steep wall. The site at about 28°N, 26°E is in a dusty region where slope streaks are common. The extreme brightness of the wall comes mostly from its slope facing the sun under low illumination from the southwest, which is consistent with the dark shadowed western wall. The concentric and contorted floor texture is typical of mid-latitude ice-related crater fill.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The wall's brightness looks partly saturated or stretched, which hides fine slope detail. From a single image, slope streaks cannot be strictly separated from recurring slope lineae or dry gully channels.
skeptic.would_refute: Repeat imaging over several years could test this. Slope streaks appear rarely and fade slowly over years. Streaks that grow and fade with the seasons would point to recurring slope lineae instead. Streaks showing incised channels with alcoves and fans in HiRISE would point to gullies.

skeptic.explanation: This is a moderately fresh simple impact crater formed in the mid-latitude plains near Deuteronilus/Arabia (about 32.5°N). The flat floor with its pitted, hummocky texture is consistent with partial infill by ice-rich mantling or fill material that has since been modified by sublimation. The relief is shown by consistent shading under western illumination: a bright eastern inner wall and a shadowed western wall. The sinuous feature to the south is a separate landform, probably an inverted channel or an eroded ridge, and is not part of the crater.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The shading on the sinuous southern feature is ambiguous. Without topography it is hard to tell whether it is a raised inverted channel or a trough wall. Its relation to the crater, if any, is unclear.
skeptic.would_refute: An elevation model showing the circular feature as a raised dome with no depression would refute the impact-crater interpretation.

skeptic.landform_class: scarp / ridge slope with slope streaks
skeptic.explanation: This is a dust-mantled, SW-facing scarp or ridge flank, probably fretted or knobby terrain near the dichotomy boundary in the Deuteronilus–Protonilus region. The bright, smooth surface is a fine dust mantle. The dark linear features are slope streaks: dry avalanches of bright dust that expose darker substrate. They start at point sources near the crest, widen and taper downslope, follow the local fall line, and occur only on the steep dusty face. The rougher, darker plateau to the NE lacks the thick dust cover.
skeptic.would_refute: An elevation model showing the bright surface is not a slope would refute this. So would repeat imaging showing the streaks stay fixed relative to the image frame (detector artifacts) rather than following the fall line, though streak orientation that changes with local slope already argues against an artifact.

skeptic.landform_class: crater rim / inner wall with slope streaks
skeptic.explanation: The dark streaks are most likely slope streaks, which are common on dust-mantled steep slopes in Arabia Terra (this site is at 26°N, 26°E). They are thought to form when a thin, bright dust layer is disturbed, through avalanching or a related mass-movement process, and slides downslope, exposing darker substrate. Several features support this: the streaks are elongate and taper at one end, they are aligned with the local downslope direction on the wall, they are confined to the steep inner wall, and the dark tone is far darker than any shadow these streaks could plausibly cast. The bright, rippled wall surface fits a thick dust or aeolian mantle draping the crater.
skeptic.does_not_fit: A few streaks look unusually crisp and saturated-dark for slope streaks at this resolution. They could partly be fresh streaks with strong contrast stretching, but this does not change the interpretation. The textured floor of the small eastern crater is not explained by slope streaks; it is likely an infill or mantle deposit.
skeptic.would_refute: Repeat imaging that showed the streaks unchanged in shape and tone over many years would weaken the slope-streak interpretation, since new streaks appear and old ones fade. So would a view under a different sun direction in which the dark features moved, which would mark them as shadows of ridges. Streaks running across the slope rather than down it in an elevation model would also argue against it.

skeptic.explanation: This is mid-latitude concentric crater fill, a debris-covered, ice-rich deposit that accumulated in the crater and flowed inward from the walls. The location (~29°N, Arabia/Deuteronilus transition) and several features fit this: the convex fill, brain-terrain texture, concentric lineations parallel to the wall, and the smooth sloping margins. The knob is probably a central peak or older floor material poking through the fill. The surrounding smooth mantle is consistent with latitude-dependent ice-rich mantling.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The fill lacks the strongly organized concentric ridge pattern typical of classic CCF. Its texture is more chaotic in the north and centre, so a partly degraded or sublimated deposit, or a different floor-fill origin, is also possible. 29°N is at the equatorward edge of where these deposits typically occur.
skeptic.would_refute: An elevation model showing the fill is flat or concave rather than convex/domed, or radar (SHARAD) showing no ice-rich subsurface, would argue against ice-rich concentric fill.

skeptic.explanation: This is a small impact crater, and the centre lies on its raised rim and proximal ejecta. Shading shows a distinct rim crest with a shadowed inner wall on the NW side. The crater has a partial fill of bright, textured material, consistent with the mantle or concentric fill commonly seen at these mid-northern latitudes on the Arabia Terra margin. The speckled, straight-edged patch east of the crater in CTX is a mosaic artifact: noisy or poorly exposed data inserted into the mosaic, not a ground feature. HiRISE shows ordinary smooth plains in the same place.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The interpretation of the floor texture as ice-related fill is less certain than the identification of the crater itself.
skeptic.would_refute: An elevation model showing no raised rim, with the circular feature lying at or above the level of the surrounding plain (for example a mound rather than a depression), would refute the crater-rim interpretation.

skeptic.explanation: This is a small, relatively young simple impact crater formed in mantled plains. Its squarish outline most likely reflects structural control by pre-existing fractures or layering in the target. The shading is consistent with illumination from the east or southeast: the wall facing the sun is bright and the opposite wall is in shadow, which marks it as a depression with a raised rim. The arcuate shadow on the floor is probably a small inner bench, a slump block, or a small superposed crater or mound.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The curved dark feature on the crater floor is not clearly resolved. It could be a slump, a central mound shadow, or a small pit.
skeptic.would_refute: An elevation model (HiRISE or CTX stereo DTM) showing the feature is a raised mound or flat-topped knob rather than a bowl-shaped depression below the surrounding plain.

skeptic.landform_class: crater rim (small impact crater with mounded interior fill)
skeptic.explanation: This is a small impact crater whose interior has been partly filled by a mound of mantle material. At ~30°N in northern Arabia Terra, this is most likely ice-rich, latitude-dependent mantle or an early stage of concentric crater fill, accumulated preferentially in the crater's cold trap. The domed, rounded fill, the narrow peripheral moat, the recurrence of the same fill in neighbouring craters, and the pitted, smoothed mantle texture of the surrounding plain all fit this regional mid-latitude mantling. The shading is consistent across the frame and there are no seams or striping, so an instrumental origin is not indicated.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The fill's brightness may be partly an albedo or contrast-stretch effect rather than purely topographic shading, so its actual height relative to the rim cannot be judged from this image alone. An alternative, a central uplift or wall-collapse mound, cannot be fully excluded at 5–6 m/pixel.
skeptic.would_refute: An elevation model (HiRISE or CTX stereo) showing the interior is a bowl-shaped depression with no convex fill would refute this. So would high-resolution imaging showing the 'mound' is bedrock or wall-collapse blocks rather than smooth, pitted mantle.

skeptic.landform_class: fault/fracture-bounded scarp (graben or trough wall) in fretted/knobby terrain
skeptic.explanation: This is a linear tectonic scarp, most likely a normal fault forming one wall of a graben or trough in the fretted terrain of the dichotomy boundary near Deuteronilus/Protonilus Mensae (about 28°N, 28°E). It has been modified by mass wasting and aeolian processes. The evidence is the straightness of the scarp, its consistent NW–SE orientation shared with parallel scarps in the context view, the angular, block-bounding geometry, and about 260 m of local relief. The dark band along the face is exposed resistant bedrock shedding boulders. The ridged deposits at its base are transverse aeolian ridges and debris trapped in the trough lee.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The images alone cannot separate fault offset from erosional enlargement of a joint or fracture, because no offset markers are visible. The rough pitted patch to the east of the context view is not explained by faulting.
skeptic.would_refute: An elevation profile across the scarp that shows matching layer elevations on both sides, with no vertical offset and only an erosional notch, would argue for an erosionally widened fracture rather than a fault scarp.

skeptic.landform_class: lineated mantled terrain (ice-rich mantle / lineated fill)
skeptic.explanation: At ~29°N in northern Arabia Terra near the dichotomy boundary, the softened topography, filled and domed craters with textured interiors, and smoothly draped relief point to the mid-latitude ice-rich mantle and associated debris fill. The aligned N–S hollows at the centre are best read as flow-parallel lineations or sublimation-enlarged grooves in this mantle, following the local downslope direction beside the sinuous ridge. The ridge may be the margin of a lobate fill or a flow ridge. Wind-sculpting of the mantle, producing yardang-like grooves, is a secondary possibility.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The lineations parallel the CTX along-track (N–S) direction, so some contribution from detector striping cannot be fully excluded, although the hollows are irregular, en echelon and variable in width, which argues for real relief. The origin of the bright sinuous ridge is uncertain: it could be a flow lobe margin, an inverted channel, or a mantle edge.
skeptic.would_refute: A HiRISE or CTX image taken with a different sun azimuth or a different ground-track orientation that shows no N–S grooves at the centre would indicate an instrumental origin. A DEM showing that the grooves cut across the local slope rather than running down it would argue against flow lineation in favour of wind erosion.

skeptic.landform_class: crater rim (impact crater with concentric/brain-terrain fill)
skeptic.explanation: An impact crater partially filled by ice-rich deposits, now expressed as concentric crater fill with brain terrain on its surface. The latitude (~29°N, Arabia Terra/Deuteronilus region margin) lies in the mid-latitude belt where lineated and concentric fill, lobate debris aprons and brain terrain are widespread, interpreted as remnants of ice-rich mantles/debris-covered ice. The domed fill pulled back from the walls with a marginal moat, the cellular closed-cell texture, and the same infill seen in neighbouring small craters all fit this. Shading is consistent with illumination from the west/southwest across the scene, so the relief reads naturally and there is no sign of seams or striping driving the pattern.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The asymmetric southeastern apron/ejecta lobe is only partly explained; it may be ejecta or flowed debris. The fill texture is near the resolution limit, so distinguishing true brain terrain from generic pitted sublimation texture is uncertain.
skeptic.would_refute: A HiRISE image or elevation model showing the floor mound is a central uplift/bedrock peak or a coherent volcanic/lava infill (e.g., layered or columnar rock without closed-cell brain texture), or a convex fill that is not elevated relative to a moat.

skeptic.landform_class: lineated mantle / viscous flow deposit on upland surface
skeptic.explanation: The surface is most likely an ice-rich debris mantle that has crept downslope, like the lineated valley fill and lobate debris aprons common along the dichotomy boundary at this latitude. Several cues support this. The lineations are smooth and curvilinear, they follow the topography, and they converge toward the scarp edge where flow would drain. They also radiate from upland alcoves in fan patterns, which is typical of flow, not of bedrock structure. The subdued, rounded appearance of the surrounding relief fits a mid-latitude mantle. Shading indicates illumination from the west: the scarp shadow falls to the east and the crater wall is dark on its western inner side, which is consistent with real topography.
skeptic.does_not_fit: Some lineations are very straight and evenly spaced, so a contribution from aeolian streaking or grooving cannot be excluded at 5–6 m per pixel. The north–south linear feature south of the crater is not clearly explained; it may be a flow boundary or a buried structure.
skeptic.would_refute: An elevation model showing that the lineations run across slope, not down it toward the scarp, would argue against flow. So would high-resolution (HiRISE) images showing them to be wind-sculpted yardangs or ripples cut into bedrock, without brain-terrain or pitted textures typical of ice-rich mantle.

skeptic.explanation: This is a small, relatively young simple impact crater formed in mantled plains at mid-northern latitude (Arabia Terra / Deuteronilus region). Its depth and bowl shape show in the strong shadowing on the sunward-facing side and the bright opposite wall. The ripple texture on the floor is most likely aeolian bedforms trapped in the crater. The nearby fainter, shallower circular forms, such as the one to the south, are older craters that are degraded or filled by mantle.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The elongate shadowed trough on the crater's NW side is not clearly explained. It could be a secondary or oblique impact, or a mantle collapse feature. Its relation to the main crater cannot be resolved here.
skeptic.would_refute: An elevation model showing the central feature standing above the plain as a dome or mound rather than lying below it as a depression would refute the crater interpretation.

skeptic.landform_class: crater with concentric/textured crater fill (ice-rich fill)
skeptic.explanation: An impact crater partly filled by ice-rich mantle material. At ~31°N in the northern mid-latitudes (Deuteronilus/Arabia margin region), mid-latitude mantle and concentric crater fill are common. That material degrades by sublimation into the pitted, 'brain-terrain'-like texture seen on the floor, and the rounded edge of the fill near the wall is typical of such deposits. The illumination is consistent between both images and across the scene, and no seams or striping cross the crater, so the pattern is a ground feature rather than an instrumental effect.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The fill looks more like a flat-topped, pitted plug than the classic concentric ridges of mature concentric crater fill. A small crater may host a thinner, less developed version, or the fill could alternatively be a degraded sediment or lava infill. The faint lobate outlines on the surrounding plains are not explained by this interpretation.
skeptic.would_refute: An elevation model showing the fill surface convex or level with the rim, with no evidence of ice. Alternatively, SHARAD or neutron data and HiRISE images showing a pit texture formed in non-volatile material (e.g., cooled lava with inflation pits) would favour a non-ice origin.

skeptic.landform_class: lineated/concentric crater fill (lobate debris fill in degraded crater)
skeptic.explanation: At ~30°N, 24°E (northern Arabia Terra, near the dichotomy fretted terrain), the smooth, pitted, lobate fill with downslope-oriented textures is best read as ice-rich mantling or debris-flow material (concentric/lineated crater fill, viscous-flow deposit) partly draping and embaying older knobs of crater floor or rim. The nearby concentric crater fill supports a regional mid-latitude ice-rich mantle. The southeast-trending tongue suggests the fill has flowed or crept out of the depression's low side. The central knobs are likely erosional remnants or buried hills protruding through the mantle. The pitting reflects sublimation degradation.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The straight, rectangular trough-ridge in the close view is unusually regular. It may be a fracture or graben in the fill, or a buried linear ridge, and is not clearly explained by flow alone. The origin of the elongate depression itself, whether an oblique impact or erosional basin, is uncertain.
skeptic.would_refute: An elevation model showing the fill is not a positive, convex-up lobate body within a depression would argue against a viscous-flow, ice-rich fill. So would SHARAD showing no low-loss ice-rich material.

skeptic.landform_class: mantled knobby terrain in a shallow valley/trough junction
skeptic.explanation: These look like eroded remnants of older highland material: knobs and short ridges left where shallow valleys or troughs converge. A dust- and ice-rich mid-latitude mantle drapes them and gives the pitted, subdued texture. Downslope creep or mass wasting of that mantle and loose debris most plausibly made the lineated, lobate surfaces south of the knobs. Shading is consistent with sun from the west. The darker tone along the NE–SW trough appears to follow the topographic low and its rougher texture rather than any image boundary. I see no seams, striping or fill that would point to an instrumental origin.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The darker tone along the NE–SW band is not fully explained. It could be a compositional or textural difference, or a subtle mosaic brightness change; this resolution cannot separate the two. Whether the lineated tongues are viscous flow or simply eroded mantle is also unresolved.
skeptic.would_refute: An elevation model showing that the knobs are not raised above the trough floor, or that the NE–SW dark band does not follow a topographic low, would undercut this reading. So would a mosaic footprint map showing the band's edges coincide with a seam between CTX frames.

skeptic.explanation: This is degraded, knobby terrain near the Arabia/dichotomy boundary that is covered by a latitude-dependent ice-rich dust mantle. The smooth bright material draped in the lows and on slopes, with faint flow-parallel lineations, and the rougher, pitted, darker texture where the mantle is thinning or sublimating fit mid-latitude mantling and possible viscous-flow modification at about 29°N. The small fresh craters are young impacts into this mantle.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The very bright, saturated-looking tone of the small craters and smooth patches is unusual. It may partly be a contrast stretch of the mosaic rather than true albedo. The close view is noisy and blurred, which limits texture interpretation.
skeptic.would_refute: A HiRISE image showing that the smooth bright material is bedrock or aeolian bedforms, with no mantle texture (no pitting, no draping), would refute this. So would an elevation model showing that the lineated lobes are not on downslope paths.

skeptic.explanation: The crater interior holds an ice-rich deposit, most likely a mid-latitude mantle or debris-covered ice. Its concentric ridges and its moat against the shaded west wall are typical of concentric crater fill. That texture forms when an ice-rich fill flows inward and partly sublimates, leaving concentric ridges. The textured, pitted mantle around it and the other infilled small craters fit the latitude-dependent ice-rich mantling widespread at this latitude. Shading shows the illumination comes from the west. The fill sits high, close to rim level, with a shadowed moat between it and the west wall, so it is a convex deposit rather than a depression.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The fill looks unusually bright and almost overfills the crater, which is somewhat more mound-like than typical concentric crater fill. The cause of the smooth south-southwest tail is uncertain: it could be wind-streak deposition in the crater's lee, or flow of mantle material.
skeptic.would_refute: An elevation model (HiRISE or CTX stereo) showing the fill surface is concave and well below the rim would argue against a convex ice-rich fill. So would HiRISE showing it is a bedrock central uplift, or a crater-floor deposit with no flow textures.

skeptic.explanation: This is a young simple impact crater formed into a smooth mantled plain. The circular planform, crisp rim and shading are consistent with a bowl: the near (west) wall is in shadow and the far (east) wall is lit, implying illumination from the west or southwest. The crater is less degraded than the surrounding subdued craters, so it postdates the mantle. The interior texture is likely slumped wall material or coarse debris. The faint vertical streaking in the close view is CTX detector or processing noise amplified by the contrast stretch, not ground texture.
skeptic.does_not_fit: No ejecta blanket or rays are clearly distinguishable from the mantle. This may reflect mantling, or the limited resolution.
skeptic.would_refute: A HiRISE image or DTM showing the feature is a positive mound rather than a depression, i.e. shading that reverses relative to other craters under the same sun, would refute the crater interpretation.

skeptic.landform_class: scarp / mesa edge slope with downslope streaks
skeptic.explanation: This is a steep scarp, probably a fretted-terrain mesa or plateau margin on the Arabia Terra dichotomy region, with a dust-mantled slope marked by slope streaks and downslope mass-wasting lineations. The slope looks very bright because it faces the sun, so its brightness comes from slope angle relative to the light, not from albedo. Several cues show the lineations are geological rather than instrumental. They are confined to the slope. They begin at the crest and point consistently downslope, following the slope's curvature. They do not continue onto the plateau or the lowland. They are not parallel to any image-wide direction, as detector striping would be. Dark and light slope streaks from small dry dust avalanches are common on dust-covered steep slopes at these latitudes.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The strong brightness of the slope approaches saturation in places. That makes it hard to tell slope streaks (an albedo feature) apart from shallow chutes or gullies (a topographic feature), and some of the contrast may be amplified by processing. A subtle tonal boundary along the base of the slope could partly reflect mosaic blending, but it does not affect the interpretation.
skeptic.would_refute: A HiRISE image or an elevation model would test this. If the lineations proved to be deep incised channels with alcoves and depositional aprons, the interpretation would shift to gullies. If the lineations appeared in a second CTX image under different sun geometry with identical tone and no relation to the slope, they would be an artifact. Repeat imaging showing new or faded dark streaks would confirm slope streaks.

skeptic.explanation: This is the rim of a large impact crater in the Arabia Terra/Deuteronilus region; the curvature over more than 10 km and the shadowed inner wall favour a crater rather than a channel or mesa edge. The bright band along the rim crest is probably exposed light-toned rim material or a dust-mantled crest. Its fine ripple-like texture is consistent with small transverse aeolian ridges or wind-eroded material collected along the topographic break. The shading is consistent with illumination from the southeast and west-facing slopes in shadow.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The small dark wedge-shaped feature east of the crest is not obviously explained. It could be a shadow cast by a small ridge, a dark slope streak, or a small image artifact. The broad curvilinear tonal boundaries on the plains to the east are also unexplained by the crater-rim interpretation alone.
skeptic.would_refute: An elevation model showing the surface northwest of the scarp is not lower than the plains, or that the curving scarp does not close into a roughly circular depression in a wider view, would refute the crater-rim interpretation.

skeptic.explanation: This is a sun-facing interior crater wall mantled by bright dust. The dark linear features are slope streaks: dust avalanches that expose darker substrate, typical of dusty mid-latitude regions such as Arabia Terra. The finer light striations are downslope grooves or dust-textured gullies on the same slope. The streaks follow the local fall line, radial to the crater, which points to downslope mass movement rather than an imaging effect.
skeptic.does_not_fit: A faint linear tonal boundary runs down the wall parallel to the rim in the close view. It could be a ledge or bench in the wall, or a subtle mosaic seam; the image does not settle which.
skeptic.would_refute: A repeat image showing the dark streaks unchanged in orientation while the slope direction differs, or streaks aligned with the detector or flight direction across terrain of varied slope, would indicate an instrumental artifact.

skeptic.landform_class: crater rim (small crater with mound-shaped interior fill)
skeptic.explanation: The most likely reading is a small impact crater whose interior has been filled by a mound of mantling deposit, probably ice-rich, with a moat left along the inner wall. The textured apron is the degraded rim and ejecta, roughened by the same mantle. Several things support this. The central body sits inside a closed depression bounded by an outer rim. The moat-and-mound arrangement matches filled craters seen in this mid-latitude band (about 29°N in Arabia Terra). Many of the smaller nearby circular knobs and rings look like smaller versions of the same filled-crater morphology. The pitted, knobby texture of the surrounding plain fits a degrading latitude-dependent mantle. No camera artifact explains it: the feature is a closed, isolated shape, and it is consistently shaded in both views with no linear striping or seam running through it.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The fill stands nearly as high as the rim and is unusually blocky and bulbous rather than showing concentric texture, so an exhumed, resistant knob ringed by a deflation moat cannot be fully excluded. The lighting direction is also ambiguous at this scale, which weakens the depression-versus-mound reading of the dark crescent.
skeptic.would_refute: An elevation model (CTX or HiRISE stereo) showing the central body rising above the surrounding plain, with no enclosing rim lower than it, would indicate a free-standing knob with a moat rather than a filled crater.

skeptic.explanation: This is concentric crater fill. Ice-rich material, probably debris-covered ice or the remains of a glacial or ice-rich mantle, has filled the crater and flowed or deformed inward. Later sublimation produced the pitted/brain-terrain surface texture and the concentric ridges parallel to the rim. The site at about 30°N in Arabia Terra/Deuteronilus-Protonilus-type mid-latitudes is typical for such ice-related fills. The arcuate central ridges look like compressional or flow folds where inward-moving fill converged.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The smoother raised lobe and the curved scarp offset to the northeast of centre are asymmetric. They may record a local collapse or an earlier fill unit, but this cannot be resolved at CTX scale.
skeptic.would_refute: Two observations would argue against an ice-rich origin: a HiRISE view showing that the knobby texture is bedrock layering with no sublimation pits or brain-terrain cells, or SHARAD/topography showing the fill is not depressed or deflated relative to the rim.

skeptic.explanation: This is most likely the eroded, retreating margin of a layered mantling deposit, typical of Arabia Terra, being stripped back from the older cratered plain. The irregular embayments and re-entrants of the scarp, the wind-streaked upper surface and the small transverse aeolian ridges banked against the bright scarp face all point to wind-driven backwasting of a friable deposit. The dark patch at the centre is best explained as a shadow cast where the scarp bends and faces away from the sun, rather than as a dark material.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The relative heights are not fully clear from shading alone. The bright band and the shadow at the bend could be read as either side being higher, so which unit stands up is uncertain. I cannot rule out that some of the darkness is a low-albedo deposit pooled in a hollow rather than pure shadow.
skeptic.would_refute: An elevation model, or an image taken under a different sun azimuth, showing no topographic step at the bend (the dark patch persists unchanged) or showing no elevation contrast between the two units would refute the scarp and shadow interpretation.

skeptic.explanation: These are transverse aeolian ridges (small dune or ripple forms) of wind-blown sediment trapped in the low floor of a degraded impact crater. The evidence is that the ridges are confined to topographic lows and occur in several separate craters. Their crestlines are regularly spaced, slightly sinuous and branching, with a consistent N–S orientation that points to a roughly E–W wind. The crater sits where the scarp of the northern unit has partly buried or embayed it, which fits the regional pattern of eroded mantling deposits and trapped sediment near the dichotomy boundary in this part of Arabia Terra/Deuteronilus.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The ridges in the southwest crater trend somewhat differently from those in the main depression. The rim of the main depression is subdued and partly merged with the scarp, so a non-impact origin for the depression cannot be fully ruled out.
skeptic.would_refute: The explanation would be refuted if higher-resolution HiRISE images showed the ridges to be polygonal fractures or brain-terrain cells in an ice-rich fill rather than asymmetric sediment bedforms, or if an elevation model showed the ridge field sitting on a raised mound rather than in a depression.

skeptic.landform_class: mantled plains with sinuous ridges/troughs at the edge of a pitted depression fill
skeptic.explanation: This is the Deuteronilus/Protonilus dichotomy-boundary region (~30°N, 30°E). The smooth bright surface is a mid-latitude ice-rich mantle or plains unit draping older terrain. The dark textured ground to the south is degraded, pitted lobate or lineated fill in a shallow basin, typical of debris-covered glacial or mantle-loss terrain. The narrow linear and sinuous features crossing the centre are most likely small ridges or troughs. They could be inverted channels, wrinkle-ridge-like fractures, or esker-like ridges partly expressed through the mantle. The shading alone does not establish whether they are raised or incised.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The short dark isolated groove south of the main lineament is ambiguous. It could be a trough segment or a shadowed scarp, and its link to the northern feature is unclear. Whether the linear features are ridges or troughs cannot be settled from a single illumination direction.
skeptic.would_refute: An elevation model (HRSC or CTX stereo DTM) showing that the bright smooth unit is not a drape, for example a lower unit lying in a depression rather than mantling the topography, would refute this. So would a DTM showing the linear features cut through bedrock with fault offsets rather than following the mantle.

skeptic.explanation: This is a young simple impact crater formed in mantled plains of the northern Arabia Terra region. Several observations support this: the bowl shape, the crisp raised rim, shading consistent with illumination from the west, and an unmodified interior aside from minor mass wasting. The fine lineations on the walls are dry ravel or small gully-like downslope features on the steep inner slopes. The darker diffuse patches on the surrounding plain are albedo variations in a thin dust or sand mantle, not relief.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The interior shading is somewhat unusual. The eastern half of the floor looks broadly bright and convex, and could hint at partial fill rather than a clean bowl, but this is within normal lighting effects for a simple crater.
skeptic.would_refute: An elevation model showing the feature as a positive mound rather than a depression with a rim would refute it. So would an image under opposite illumination that inverted the shading in a way inconsistent with a bowl.

skeptic.landform_class: degraded/pitted mantle on plateau or depression floor (knobby textured terrain)
skeptic.explanation: At ~30°N in the Deuteronilus/Protonilus-type fretted terrain zone, this looks like ice-rich latitude-dependent mantle and lineated fill that has been partially stripped or sublimated. That left a knobby, pitted 'brain-like' texture where the smooth cover is gone, with smooth intact mantle surviving on the slopes and in the south. Shading is consistent with real relief: knobs show consistent illumination and craters have normal shadowing, so this is not an instrumental pattern.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The rough patch's fairly straight, rectangular outline is not explained. It could reflect a structural or topographic boundary, or possibly differing image lighting in the mosaic. There is also the bright, washed-out area in the lower right, which may be a slope facing the sun or a contrast difference between mosaic frames.
skeptic.would_refute: An elevation model showing the rough patch is a positive, resistant layer (for example lava or an eroded bedrock surface) rather than a degraded mantle surface. Alternatively, an overlapping image showing that the rectangular boundary is a mosaic seam with no texture change.

skeptic.explanation: This is old cratered plain draped by a smooth-to-pitted mantle, most likely the mid-latitude, ice-rich latitude-dependent mantle that is common near 30–35°N along the dichotomy-boundary region. The mantle softens and partly buries small craters, which accounts for the ghost-like circular hollows. The same mantle fills larger craters with flat floors carrying a pitted, possibly sublimation-roughened texture. The few sharp small craters are younger impacts that postdate the mantle. Shading is consistent with sunlight from the west, and there are no seams, stripes or fill artifacts at the centre.
skeptic.does_not_fit: At ~5–6 m per pixel it cannot be confirmed whether the fine pitting is sublimation texture or just noise and small craters. The ice content of the mantle cannot be shown from these images.
skeptic.would_refute: Higher-resolution images (HiRISE) showing bare, unmantled bedrock or lava-flow textures with no draping layer and no sublimation pits, or an elevation model showing the crater fills are not elevated or flat but bowl-shaped, would refute a mantle origin.

skeptic.landform_class: lobate debris apron / lineated valley fill
skeptic.explanation: At ~30°N in the Deuteronilus–Protonilus Mensae fretted terrain, this is ice-rich viscous-flow material (lobate debris aprons and lineated valley fill, likely debris-covered glacial ice) that has flowed from alcoves in the surrounding massifs into the trough; its pitted, brain-like texture reflects sublimation and degradation of an ice-rich surface, and the same material forms concentric crater fill in the crater to the south.
skeptic.would_refute: SHARAD radar showing no subsurface reflector/low-loss ice signature beneath the fill, or an elevation model showing the fill does not slope away from the alcoves and wall bases.

skeptic.landform_class: lobate debris apron / mesa margin scarp
skeptic.explanation: This is most likely the steep terminal margin of an elevated, lineated deposit, such as a lobate debris apron or the ice-rich mantle of a mesa in the fretted terrain at the northern edge of Arabia Terra. Several features point to a real edge that stands above the plains. The surface lineations converge toward the margin, consistent with downslope flow. The edge has a bright rim. A dark shadow lies just outside it on the lower terrain. The boundary is curved and follows the topography rather than running straight like a mosaic seam.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The body is brighter than the plains by an unusually large and nearly uniform amount. Slope facing alone does not obviously account for that. Part of the contrast could come from mosaic tone balancing or from images taken under different illumination joined along this edge.
skeptic.would_refute: An elevation model (CTX stereo or MOLA) showing no topographic step at the edge would refute this. So would source CTX images showing that the brightness boundary coincides with a footprint edge between two images, in which case it would be a mosaic seam rather than a scarp.

skeptic.explanation: Most likely a mid-latitude impact crater partly filled by a mantle or crater-fill deposit (likely ice-related). The small fresh craters nearby are dark on their west inner walls and bright on their east walls, which implies sun from the west. On that basis, the dark western crescent and bright eastern band of the central feature are best read as the inner walls of a bowl-shaped crater. The central textured disc would then be a fill deposit on the floor, with the pitted, knobby texture of degraded ice-rich mantle or concentric crater fill. That texture is common at about 29°N in northern Arabia Terra, and the softened appearance of the surrounding plains fits a regional mantle.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The shading could also be read as a raised pedestal or mound with a pit on top, especially with the bright, apron-like eastern band and the lumpy northern edge. The sun direction is inferred only from small craters, so I cannot rule out a positive-relief form. The fill's exact relief (domed versus flat) and the origin of its pitted texture cannot be resolved at about 5-6 m per pixel.
skeptic.would_refute: An elevation model (CTX stereo DTM or MOLA) showing the outer annulus standing above the surrounding plains as a mound, rather than dipping below them as a crater bowl, would refute the filled-crater reading.

skeptic.explanation: These are impact craters partly filled by ice-rich mantle or concentric crater fill. The fill surface has been roughened by sublimation and degradation into pitted, cellular 'brain terrain' texture. This style is common at about 30–45°N, where a latitude-dependent, ice-rich mantle and glacial-like fill accumulate in topographic lows. The domed fill, the smooth mantled surroundings, and the repetition of the same texture in several nearby depressions all fit this deposit type. The lighting is consistent across the views and there are no seams or striping, so an instrumental cause is not indicated.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The latitude (31°N) is near the equatorward limit for such fill, and the cellular texture is less clearly organised into brain-terrain ridges than is typical. It could instead be a degraded lag or boulder-rich surface.
skeptic.would_refute: Two kinds of evidence would argue against an ice-rich origin. HiRISE imaging could show the knobby texture to be loose boulders or bedrock blocks rather than sublimation pits or brain-terrain cells. SHARAD could show no shallow ice-consistent radar reflector or dielectric signature in the fill.

skeptic.explanation: The location is most likely the floor of a shallow NW–SE trending trough or channel at about 30°N in the Arabia/Deuteronilus region. It carries faint flow-parallel lineations, which could come from ice-related viscous flow fill, from fluvial or aeolian scour, or both, and it is covered by a mid-latitude mantle that subdues small-scale relief. The orientation of the lineations follows the trough walls. The dark band along the SW edge is a shadowed wall or scarp, consistent with illumination from the left.
skeptic.does_not_fit: Several small craters appear bright and puffy, almost convex, which may be a stretch or saturation effect or mantled infill rather than true relief. The close view's speckled noise hides fine texture, so it cannot confirm lineated valley fill as opposed to wind streaks.
skeptic.would_refute: An elevation model (CTX or HRSC DTM) showing the centre is not topographically lower than its surroundings, or that the lineations do not parallel any slope, would refute the trough or valley-fill interpretation.

skeptic.landform_class: crater floor fill (degraded impact crater with mantled/lobate fill)
skeptic.explanation: This is an impact crater whose floor has been partly infilled. The fill is most likely ice-rich mantling or debris material typical of the ~30°N latitude band near Arabia Terra–Deuteronilus, and it gives a hummocky, concentric-to-lobate floor. Mass wasting from the walls, including the small alcoves on the inner wall, has added to it. The relief cues are consistent: the western wall is in shadow and the eastern wall is lit, which fits a bowl under western illumination. The softened, mantled texture of both the floor and the surroundings fits regional latitude-dependent mantle deposits.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The small central sinuous ridge or scarp feature is not clearly explained; it could be an eroded remnant or a fill boundary. Only one image is available, so the composition of the fill (ice-rich or not) cannot be confirmed.
skeptic.would_refute: A HiRISE or CTX elevation model showing the floor at the original fresh-crater depth (no significant fill), or high-resolution images lacking concentric or brain-terrain textures, would weaken the ice-rich fill interpretation.

skeptic.explanation: This is a degraded impact crater rim mantled by a smooth, probably dust- or ice-rich deposit of the kind common across mid-latitude Arabia Terra. Lighting appears to come from the west. The inner west wall is in shadow while the inner east wall at the centre is brightly lit, which is consistent with a raised rim and a depressed interior. The mantle subdues the rim crest and ejecta and fills the floor. The pitted texture along the lower south wall is likely erosion or sublimation of that mantle. The vertical streaks and speckle in the close view are detector noise and resampling artifacts from enlarging the CTX data, not ground features.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The exact origin of the pitted, knobby texture on the south wall cannot be resolved at this scale. It could be mantle degradation or exposed rim material.
skeptic.would_refute: An elevation model showing no raised rim and no interior depression at the centre would refute this. So would an image under eastern illumination in which the bright and dark wall pattern did not reverse.

skeptic.explanation: This is most likely an aeolian albedo feature. Wind has thinned or removed bright dust from a dust-mantled plain in northern Arabia Terra, exposing darker or rougher underlying mantle material. Three things support this: the margins are gradational, the internal lineations are consistently aligned with the patch elongation (NNW–SSE, the inferred wind direction), and the darkening cuts across terrain without following crater or slope boundaries. Some of the darkening may come from subtle shading of shallow grooves or troughs, but the tone change is mainly albedo. A mosaic seam is unlikely because the boundaries are irregular, diffuse and not straight, and they are consistent between both views.
skeptic.does_not_fit: Part of the darkness could be topographic shading of a gentle depression or a grooved slope rather than albedo. The brightness of the small craters (they appear as bright domes) is not explained by dust removal alone and may reflect mantled or infilled craters.
skeptic.would_refute: A CTX image of the same spot under a different sun azimuth, or a different season. If the dark patch shifts or reverses with lighting, it is topographic shading rather than albedo. If it is a sharp-edged band matching an image footprint, it is a mosaic seam. An elevation model showing a trough coincident with the dark area would also favour shading.

skeptic.landform_class: crater with fill (in a mid-latitude valley)
skeptic.explanation: An impact crater whose interior has been partly filled by pitted, knobby material that is likely ice-rich mantle or concentric-crater-fill-type deposits. These are common at ~30°N in the Arabia/Deuteronilus region. Mid-latitude ice-rich mantling and its sublimation-driven degradation give the pitted floor and the pitted patch on the adjacent valley wall. The valley itself is an older trough or channel that has been mantled by smooth lobate deposits. The rim relief, shadowing and bright sunlit walls are consistent with a real topographic depression lit from the west.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The crater's slightly angular outline and the very dark tone of the trough floor are not fully explained. They could reflect jointed target material and a local albedo or roughness difference rather than shading alone.
skeptic.would_refute: An elevation model showing the crater floor at or above the surrounding plain would refute the reading of a partially filled impact crater, as would evidence that it is instead a rimless collapse pit or a positive-relief feature.

skeptic.landform_class: lineated valley fill / lobate debris apron surface
skeptic.explanation: This is lineated, ice-rich viscous-flow material: either lineated valley fill or debris apron surface. The location at 32°N in the Deuteronilus/Protonilus fretted terrain (near Mamers Valles) is typical for such deposits. The parallel ridges and troughs, the flow-parallel striations, the pitted 'brain-like' texture and the soft, mantled appearance all fit glacial-like flow of debris-covered ice, later modified by sublimation.
skeptic.does_not_fit: Some of the ridges look like bedrock spurs or ribs of a fretted valley wall rather than flow lineations. At this scale, scarp-wall morphology cannot be fully separated from fill.
skeptic.would_refute: An elevation model showing that the lineations do not follow downslope or down-valley flow paths. Alternatively, SHARAD radar showing no ice-rich subsurface beneath the ridged material.

skeptic.explanation: The centre is the outer edge of a crater-floor fill deposit where it meets the trough at the foot of the crater wall. The deposit could be sedimentary or ice-cemented mantle material of the kind common in Arabia Terra craters. The ribbed band along its edge is most likely erosional texture on the exposed fill margin, or small aeolian bedforms trapped against it. Relief cues from the sun on the left support a real step in topography. The scarp throws a shadow-side edge, and nearby small craters show normal bowl shading. The terraced wall above is consistent with retreat of the wall or of the fill in stages. The texture is continuous across both images, follows the curved margin, and shows no straight seams or along-track striping, so an instrumental origin is unlikely.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The images cannot tell apart wind-sculpted ridges, ice-loss texture in the fill, and a fine-scale lineated debris flow. Why the ridges are confined to a narrow marginal band, rather than covering the whole floor, is also unexplained. The ridge orientation relative to the curved margin is hard to judge at this resolution.
skeptic.would_refute: HiRISE imaging showing the marginal ridges to be dune-like bedforms that cross the deposit edge onto the trough floor would undercut the fill-erosion interpretation. An elevation model showing the trough at the same height as the fill surface, rather than lower, would undercut the marginal-scarp reading.

skeptic.landform_class: crater (small fresh impact crater on textured plains)
skeptic.explanation: This is a small, relatively young simple impact crater on mid-latitude plains near Arabia Terra and the Deuteronilus region at about 31°N. Several features support an impact origin: the sharp raised rim, the circular plan, and a shadow on the west wall that is consistent with a depression lit from the west. The flat floor suggests partial infilling, possibly ice-rich mantle or debris. The roughened, pitted surrounding texture fits a degraded latitude-dependent mantle. The nearby rounded bright features are smaller, more degraded or infilled craters.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The flat, textured floor is shallow for a fresh simple crater. This could be infill, or a concentric or layered target, and cannot be resolved at this scale.
skeptic.would_refute: An elevation model showing the feature as a positive-relief mound rather than a depression with a raised rim, or a second image under opposite illumination in which the shadow did not move to the opposite wall.

skeptic.explanation: A small, relatively young simple impact crater formed on a smooth plains/infill unit that ponded in topographic lows within older knobby, mantled terrain of the Arabia/dichotomy-region type. The crisp, continuous rim and well-defined shadow on the sun-facing-away wall indicate a bowl with raised rim. Its flat-looking floor suggests partial infill or a shallow depth, possibly controlled by a resistant layer. The smooth host unit, with its stippled micro-texture, is likely a sedimentary or volcanic fill or a mantle deposit, and is younger than the surrounding knobs.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The floor appears unusually flat for a fresh simple crater of this size. This could reflect shallow infill or a layered target, but cannot be resolved at CTX scale.
skeptic.would_refute: An elevation model (e.g., a CTX stereo DTM) showing the circle has no raised rim or no depression, e.g. a positive pedestal or mesa, would refute an impact-crater interpretation.

skeptic.explanation: This is a relatively young simple impact crater formed in a mantled plains surface in the Arabia Terra region. The sharp rim, deep bowl and strong shadowing indicate little degradation compared with the many softened, mantle-filled craters around it. The pitted texture on the northern ejecta/rim apron is plausibly ejecta or a rim deposit roughened by sublimation or deflation, or secondary pitting. The adjacent shallow depression to the southeast is probably an older, infilled crater that the new impact partly overlaps.
skeptic.does_not_fit: The pitted patch is confined to the north/northeast side rather than forming a symmetric ejecta blanket, and its origin is not resolved at CTX scale.
skeptic.would_refute: An elevation model showing no depression, or a raised dome instead of a bowl, at the centre would refute the impact-crater interpretation. A second image with opposite sun azimuth showing the shading does not reverse would do the same.
